title: CBSE Class 8 Maths Case Studies — Chapter-wise Guide + Practice
meta_title: CBSE Class 8 Maths Case Studies: Chapter Guide
meta_desc: What CBSE Class 8 Maths case studies are, the chapters they test and a 4-step method to crack them, plus a free 8-question quiz and practice e-book.
excerpt: Case-study questions trip up strong Class 8 students not because the maths is hard, but because the sums are buried in a paragraph. Here is what they are, which chapters they pull from, and a four-step method that works every time.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A Class 8 student who can solve 40 rational-number sums in a row will still freeze when the same arithmetic shows up wrapped inside a five-line story about a shopkeeper and a discount. That freeze is the whole point of a case study — and it is exactly why so many otherwise strong students lose easy marks on them. The maths hidden inside a CBSE Class 8 Maths case study is almost never above grade level. The difficulty is in reading a real situation and deciding which sum to do. This guide walks through what these questions actually are, why the board leans on them now, the chapters they draw from, and a four-step method I use with students to turn a scary paragraph into three quick marks.

What a case-study question really is

A case study is a short passage — a paragraph, a small table, sometimes a diagram — describing a real or realistic situation, followed by three to five sub-questions that get harder as they go. The first sub-question is usually a direct read-off (‘How many students chose cricket?’). The middle ones ask you to calculate. The last one often asks you to reason or justify (‘Was the shopkeeper’s claim correct? Why?’).

The board calls these competency-based or case-based questions, and they are not a gimmick. They test whether a child can move from a messy real-world description to the clean piece of maths underneath it. That single skill — translation — is what separates a student who has memorised a formula from one who understands it.

Why CBSE added them

For years, Indian board papers rewarded pattern-matching: see the word ‘area’, plug into the area formula. The National Education Policy 2020 pushed hard against exactly that, asking for assessment of understanding over rote recall. From the 2021–22 session onward, CBSE mandated that a fixed share of marks in every subject come from competency-based items. For Maths, that means a meaningful chunk of your Class 8 paper is now case studies, and ignoring them is no longer an option.

The honest upside for students: these questions are more predictable than they look. Once you know the four-step method, the paragraph stops being an obstacle.

The Class 8 chapters case studies love

Case studies pull from chapters that naturally connect to daily life, so a handful of NCERT chapters show up far more than the rest. Knowing which ones lets you practise smart.

  • Comparing Quantities — discounts, profit and loss, simple and compound interest, GST. This is the single most common case-study source because shopping and money are everywhere.
  • Mensuration — area of trapeziums and polygons, surface area and volume of cubes, cuboids and cylinders. Think water tanks, tiled floors, and cardboard boxes.
  • Data Handling — bar graphs, pie charts, and simple probability drawn from a survey or a spinner.
  • Linear Equations in One Variable — age problems, mixture and cost situations where you must first form the equation.
  • Rational Numbers — sharing, measurement, and number-line reasoning set in a real context.
  • Exponents and Powers — standard form for very large or very small quantities, like distances in space or the size of a cell.

A four-step method to crack any case study

The same routine works whether the passage is about a cricket survey or a cylindrical water tank. Do it in order and do not skip step one.

StepWhat you doWhy it matters
1. Read for the askRead the sub-question first, then the passageYou read the story looking for specific numbers, not blindly
2. List the dataJot every number with its unit in the marginStops unit slips (cm vs m) and reveals what is missing
3. Name the conceptDecide the one chapter/formula the sub-question needsTurns a paragraph into a familiar textbook sum
4. Solve and sanity-checkCompute, then ask ‘does this answer make sense?’A volume of 2 litres for a swimming pool signals an error

A worked example

Here is a typical Comparing Quantities case study. A shopkeeper marks a school bag at ₹1,200 and offers a 15% discount. A customer also has to pay 5% GST on the discounted price.

Q: What is the final amount the customer pays?

Step 1, the ask: the final price after discount and then GST. Step 2, the data: marked price ₹1,200, discount 15%, GST 5%. Step 3, the concept: percentage of a quantity, applied twice in sequence. Step 4, solve. Discount = 15% of ₹1,200 = ₹180, so the discounted price is ₹1,020. GST = 5% of ₹1,020 = ₹51. Final amount = ₹1,020 + ₹51 = ₹1,071. Sanity check: it is below the marked price but above the discounted price, which is exactly what discount-then-tax should give.

Notice that the hardest part was never the arithmetic. It was catching that GST applies to the discounted price, not the original — a detail hidden in one word of the passage. That is the whole game.

How to practise so it sticks

Do not practise case studies by reading solved ones. That builds recognition, not skill. Instead, cover the solution, attempt the full set of sub-questions on paper, and only then check. In my experience the students who improve fastest are the ones who mark where they went wrong — misread the ask, wrong formula, or a careless calculation — because each of those has a different fix. Aim for two or three complete case studies a day in the fortnight before an exam rather than a marathon the night before.

Try the quiz, then the full practice set

quiz.title: Class 8 Maths Case Study Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight case-study style questions across comparing quantities, mensuration, data handling and more. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A shirt marked ₹800 is sold at a 25% discount. What is the selling price?
A shopkeeper buys a fan for ₹1,500 and sells it for ₹1,800. What is the profit percent?
A cuboidal tank is 2 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m high. How many litres does it hold when full? (1 m³ = 1000 L)
A trapezium-shaped field has parallel sides 20 m and 12 m, and the distance between them is 10 m. What is its area?
In a survey of 200 students, 90 chose cricket. What angle represents cricket in a pie chart?
Five years from now Ravi will be 3 times as old as he was 5 years ago. His present age (in years) satisfies which equation?
questions.explanation: Age in 5 years is x + 5; age 5 years ago is x - 5; the first is 3 times the second: x + 5 = 3(x - 5).

questions.q: A price of ₹1,000 rises by 10% one year and then by 10% again the next. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: Year 1: 1000 + 10% = 1100. Year 2: 1100 + 10% = 1210. This is compound growth, not a flat 20%.

questions.q: The diameter of a human hair is about 0.00007 m. Written in standard form, this is:
questions.explanation: 0.00007 = 7 × 10⁻⁵, since the decimal point moves 5 places to the right.

faq.q: How many case-study questions come in the Class 8 Maths exam?
faq.a: It varies by school and year, but competency-based questions (which include case studies) make up a fixed, board-mandated share of the paper — typically several marks worth. Treat them as guaranteed, not optional.

faq.q: Which Class 8 chapter has the most case studies?
faq.a: Comparing Quantities, by a clear margin — discount, profit and loss, interest and GST map neatly onto everyday money situations. Mensuration and Data Handling come next.

faq.q: Are case-study questions harder than normal questions?
faq.a: The arithmetic is usually the same grade level. The extra difficulty is reading the situation and choosing the right formula. Once you can translate the passage into a plain sum, the marks come easily.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake students make in case studies?
faq.a: Reading the passage before the question, then solving the wrong thing. Read the sub-question first, then hunt the passage for the exact numbers it needs.
